stories.headline: Sydney police step up armed patrols after Bondi terror attack
stories.title: Sydney police step up armed patrols after Bondi terror attack
stories.summary: Sydney, Oct 8 : Heavily armed police will be deployed across Australia's Sydney ahead of a rapid response unit established in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack becoming fully operational. The government of the Australian state of New South Wales (NSW) on Thursday said that officers from the state police force's new Armed Response Command (ARC) will begin patrolling Sydney over the coming weeks as the unit's training moves into realistic environments. The ARC was established as a permanent unit by the state government following the fatal mass shooting of 15 people at a Jewish holiday celebration at Bondi Beach in December last year, Xinhua News Agency reported. NSW Premier Chris Minns, Police and Counter-terrorism Minister Yasmin Catley and Police Commissioner Mal Lanyon said in a statement on Thursday that ARC officers will patrol high-risk areas, including places of worship and major events, and rapidly respond to emerging threats. The 250-officer unit will have access to combat assault rifles and 24 purpose-built vehicles and will be supported by a specialised operations centre. "Keeping the people of New South Wales safe is our number one priority. That means making sure our police have the people, training and equipment they need to respond to serious threats," Minns said. Lanyon said that the ARC would act as a deterrent for anyone who wishes to commit harm, incite hatred or cause fear. In February, accused Bondi Beach terror attack perpetrator Naveed Akram made his first appearance in a Sydney court after being charged with 59 offences over the fatal mass shooting. Akram appeared on Monday morning via video link from a supermax prison where he has been held since being discharged from the hospital in the wake of the attack on December 14, 2025. The 24-year-old was charged with 59 offences, including 15 counts of murder and one count of committing a terrorist act, in relation to the attack. Authorities allege that Akram and his father, Sajid, who was shot dead by police at the scene of the attack, opened fire on a Jewish celebration at the iconic eastern Sydney beach using rifles and shotguns, killing 15 people and injuring dozens more. Court documents made public in December 2025 revealed that police found evidence that the two attackers had conducted firearms training at a rural property before the attack. Local media reported that Akram was mostly silent during the administrative hearing and only spoke when directly addressed by the presiding Magistrate. --IANS

stories.headline: Mint Explainer: Why is Elon Musk’s Starlink at war with Indian telecom giants?
stories.title: Mint Explainer: Why is Elon Musk’s Starlink at war with Indian telecom giants?
stories.summary: Elon Musk claims Indian ‘oligarchs’ are stalling Starlink’s launch, deepening a fierce battle with Jio and Airtel over spectrum allocation and market control.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: On Wednesday, a post from SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk, who has 241.6 million followers on X, sparked a new battle involving the satellite firm, the Indian telecom sector, and the government.

Musk alleged that Indian “oligarchs” were scuttling Starlink’s launch in the country to maintain a “monopolistic chokehold on the Indian people.” While he named no individuals or companies, the troika commanding the Indian telecom industry comprises Reliance Jio Infocomm, Bharti Airtel, and Vodafone Idea.
By Thursday morning, the government refuted any suggestions of bias as “baseless and misconceived”.
Mint explains the satellite wars now engulfing India’s telecom industry.
How did the battle lines get drawn?

Starlink registered its business in India in 2021 and began advertising and preselling its services until the government stepped in, saying the company lacked a license and could not presell satellite connections without regulatory approval.
That marked the start of a long-drawn-out war between the US firm and its Indian rivals.
Starlink reapplied for the license in 2022 and eventually secured it last year.
OneWeb India was the first to receive the global mobile personal communications by satellite (GMPCS) licence in April 2022, followed by Jio Satellite in October 2022, and Starlink in June 2025.

More than four years after India issued the first license for satellite internet services, commercial launches for all players remain stalled due to security concerns and mistrust surrounding foreign satellite operators.
What is stalling approvals for satellite operators?
Awaiting the final nod are Elon Musk-owned Starlink, Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb, and Jio Satellite Communications Ltd, a wholly owned subsidiary of Jio Platforms.

article_sentences: West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Thursday (October 8, 2026) said his government will provide ₹1.8 lakh aid for fully damaged homes and ₹90,000 for partially affected houses in flood-hit Malda district.

Speaking at a flood-relief distribution programme at Raghunathpur, Mr. Adhikari also said that IIT-Kanpur has been tasked with preparing a detailed project report (DPR) for a permanent flood solution in Malda.
“Proposals have been sent to the Centre seeking ₹3,300 crore projects for river erosion control in Malda and Murshidabad.
Projects worth ₹500 crore have been cleared,” he said.
“Previous governments did not resolve the flood problem in areas like Bhutni, parts of Ratua and villages in English Bazar in Malda.
But, we will work out a permanent solution to the flood issue in Malda,” the CM asserted.

stories.summary: Justice V. Lakshminarayanan wants to know how Mr. Vijay would overcome the Supreme Court rulings on the subject

article_sentences: The hearing on Chief Minister C. Joseph Vijay’s plea to reject an election petition filed against his victory from the Perambur constituency took an interesting turn on Wednesday (October 7, 2026), with Justice V. Lakshminarayanan of the Madras High Court remarking that the entire texture of the case had changed in view of the Supreme Court judgments cited by counsel for the election petitioner.

After hearing the arguments made on behalf of the Chief Minister on Monday and Tuesday, the Judge began firing a volley of questions at the election petitioner’s counsel on Wednesday (October 7, 2026), asking how some alleged discrepancies in assets worth over ₹600 crore declared by Mr. Vijay would amount to undue influence over voters or could be termed as a corrupt electoral practice.

The Judge wanted to know whether the voters in the Perambur constituency would have been swayed in one direction or the other simply because there was a difference of a few crores or a few lakhs in the assets declared by the Chief Minister, especially in light of the fact that he was a “superstar” in the cinema industry and had voluntarily declared both movable and immovable properties worth more than ₹600 crore.
The Judge said he had relied on a chartered accountant to declare his assets while being elevated to the position of a Judge of the High Court.

Therefore, if Mr. Vijay had also declared his assets through a chartered accountant, how could his election itself be declared null and void for any mistakes made by the auditor in such a declaration, the Judge wondered.

He also questioned the challenge made by a voter, S. Dinesh, through his counsel on record, V.R. Shanmuganathan, to the election of the Chief Minister from Perambur on the ground of improper acceptance of the nomination form by the Returning Officer concerned.
The Judge wanted to know how the Returning Officer could be expected to verify the correctness of the declared assets.

In answering the questions, the election petitioner’s counsel said that the Returning Officer was expected to conduct only a summary inquiry, whereas the charge of false declaration, and whether such declaration was made wilfully and deliberately, could be inquired into only by means of leading evidence during the course of trial in an election petition.
Hence, the election petition should not be rejected at the threshold, he argued.

He said, Justice V. Ramasubramanian (during his stint in the Madras High Court before his retirement as a Supreme Court Judge) had in Krishnamoorthy versus Sivakumar (2009) held that “any incorrect information, wrong information, incomplete information, false information, one-sided information, disinformation, misinformation and non-information would certainly interfere with the free exercise of the electoral right of the voter, inasmuch as his choice of candidate will be influenced greatly by the information so furnished or withheld.”
“The view taken by Justice Ramasubramanian was affirmed by the Supreme Court in 2015.
Therefore, I have made out a cause of action for the trial of the election petition and it should not be rejected in limine,” the counsel said.

stories.headline: Plea In Supreme Court Challenges Appointment Of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Sandhu & Vivek Joshi
stories.title: Plea In Supreme Court Challenges Appointment Of CEC Gyanesh Kumar, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Sandhu & Vivek Joshi
stories.summary: The petitioner alleges that the appointments are carried out in violation of the procedure laid down under the 2023 Act.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The petitioner alleges that the appointments are carried out in violation of the procedure laid down under the 2023 Act.

A petition has been filed before the Supreme Court seeking writs of quo warranto against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, alleging that their appointments were made in breach of the procedure prescribed under the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023.
The writ petition, filed under Article 32 by Suri Payala, challenges the March 14, 2024 notifications which appointed Gyanesh Kumar and Sukhbir Singh Sandhu as Election Commissioners.

The petition further challenges Gyanesh Kumar's appointment as the CEC through the notification dated February 17, 2025, and Vivek Joshi's appointment as Election Commissioner through the same notification.
The petitioner alleges non-compliance with Sections 5, 6 and 8(1) of the Act in the appointments.
Referring to Section 6, the petitioner argues that the Search Committee was required to prepare a panel of five persons for each vacancy.
However, when two Election Commissioner vacancies arose in March 2024, the Search Committee recommended only six names for the two vacancies.
The petition relies on the Supreme Court's March 22, 2024 order in the plea challenging the 2023 Act, in which the Court had observed that Section 6 required ten names for two vacancies.

In the said order, the Court had also expressed concerns over the hasty procedure, and said that appointments must be done only after circulating the full detials of the names with the selection committee members.
According to the petitioner, this raises the question whether the six names constituted a "panel" prepared by the Search Committee in the manner contemplated by Section 6.

Section 5 of the 2023 Act restricts eligibility to persons who hold or have held a post equivalent to Secretary to the Government of India and are persons of integrity with knowledge of and experience in the management and conduct of elections.
Section 8(1) requires the Selection Committee to regulate its procedure in a transparent manner.

stories.headline: Microfinance's reckoning: Can India's lenders grow without repeating the past?
stories.title: Microfinance's reckoning: Can India's lenders grow without repeating the past?
stories.summary: For years, India's microfinance industry ran on the formula of lending small amounts to millions of low-income households, keeping collections high, adding borrowers and branches and letting scale do the rest. The model made microfinance one of the country's most important channels of formal credit for households conventional banks found too expensive to serve.After surviving the Covid-19 pandemic, the industry entered the post-pandemic period with confidence. Demand returned strongly, capital was plentiful, new players entered and competition for borrowers intensified. “Microfinance institutions were mono-line businesses for a long time due to regulatory prescription," says Ganesh Narayanan, CEO and MD of CreditAccess Grameen. The problem was not just an external shock hitting an otherwise sound business; it was perhaps the first time, the sector itself had begun to overheat.Lenders competed for customers already borrowing from several institutions, and indebtedness accumulated beneath what still looked like healthy growth. At the peak, around a quarter of CreditAccess Grameen's AUM was linked to borrowers with exposure to more than three lenders; that figure is now around 2 percent.The warning signs were visible in credit-bureau data, but the industry was slow to act. When collections deteriorated in 2024, the first explanations were external—heat waves, elections, campaigns against indebtedness.Then came the Karza Mukti Abhiyan and legislative intervention, most notably in Karnataka. What looked like temporary disturbances exposed a deeper vulnerability: Credit had grown faster than the industry's ability to assess a household's total repayment capacity. However, not all credit stress is the same. A borrower hit by a drought can recover once the shock passes; a household that has taken on debt beyond what it can service faces a different problem entirely.The industry spent much of the downturn figuring out which it was dealing with. By the time leverage emerged as the bigger issue, lenders were already facing higher credit costs, weaker collections, tighter funding and a sceptical investor base.In response, underwriting tightened, scrutiny of household indebtedness increased, and borrower-level monitoring strengthened. By mid-2026, around 98 percent of borrowers were within the industry's lender-count limits meaning no borrower can borrow from more than three lenders.ICRA reports a meaningful reduction in overleveraging—95 percent of borrowers now have exposure to three lenders or fewer. It expects assets under management growth to rebound to 15-17 per cent in FY27. But with cleaner credit metrics, can these businesses generate attractive returns without eventually recreating the same problem?With a bit of caution in mind, Gautam Trivedi, co-founder and managing partner at Nepean Capital, says, "We will stay away from these stocks.” In his view, some of the industry's difficulties are structural rather than cyclical—borrowers stacking multiple loans, weak enforceability, and the risk of legislative intervention, like Karnataka showed.Also Read: How No-Cost-EMIs have changed the way Indians shopBorrowers Still ExistIndia's low-income households still need working capital, emergency finance, and money for housing and small businesses.Moneylenders still operate alongside formal institutions, proof that demand in this segment far exceeds what the formal MFI industry serves. Venkatesh Krishnan, CEO of Spandana Sphoorty, believes this is why microfinance will remain relevant for decades. What has changed is the borrower. A customer who enters the system with a Rs 30,000 joint-liability loan won't stay a microfinance customer forever.As income and business needs grow, so does demand. For the lender, instead of constantly acquiring new borrowers, it can retain the ones it already knows and grow the relationship.The scale of that opportunity shows at CreditAccess Grameen. Its existing customers have borrowed roughly Rs 83,000 crore from other lenders while its own "graduation" portfolio—where customers borrow outside of microfinance—is only around Rs 5,600 crore as of June 2026.This implies that the industry's future may lie less in finding millions of new borrowers than in following existing customers as their needs evolve. That's a reshaping strategy, rather than staying pure-play joint-liability lenders, MFIs want to become broader financial-services companies serving the same customer across life stages.Regulation has helped too. In June 2025, the RBI cut the qualifying-asset requirement for NBFC-MFIs from 75 percent to 60 percent of total assets, giving them room to diversify. This means that lenders can now have 40 percent of their loans outside microfinance compared to 25 percent earlier.CreditAccess Grameen wants roughly half its business from non-MFI activities by 2031, with 20-30 percent of its portfolio in secured loans. Spandana is keeping joint-liability lending as its core while expanding individual loans and loans against property.Across the sector, lenders are talking about migrating customers to secured products and using data to spot borrowers capable of larger loans. The challenge is distinguishing a borrower whose income has genuinely grown from one whose apparent capacity simply reflects more debt. That may be the central lesson of the downturn: growth alone is no longer enough.Also Read: Why retailers love buy now, pay laterThe Economics Have To ChangeThe real test now isn't whether loan growth returns. It’s whether lenders can grow while producing acceptable returns through an entire credit cycle, a much higher bar than before.The numbers offer a sobering baseline. According to Alok Misra, CEO of the Micro Finance Industry Network (MFIN), the top 15 microfinance companies generated average ROA of about 2.2 percent and ROE of roughly 8.5 percent between 2016 and 2024—a period that includes Covid's disruption.MFIN believes a well-run microfinance business should generate around 3.5 percent ROA and 15-16 percent return on equity over a cycle. Returns of 20-22 percent, while possible in good years, are unlikely to be sustainable without taking on more risk.That creates a balancing act. The strongest players have spent years building distribution networks and field forces that are valuable but operationally heavy.With pricing competitive and credit costs still elevated, margin is limited, and charging borrowers more isn't really an option. Even though pricing has been deregulated, it stays politically sensitive. The more durable path is improving productivity, using technology better, and deepening each customer relationship—which is where diversification comes in.The RBI's June 2025 rule change lets lenders hold up to 40 percent of their books outside microfinance, effectively turning microfinance into a customer-acquisition engine rather than the whole business.Gold loans, individual loans, housing finance and MSME lending offer larger ticket sizes and different risk profiles, reducing the earnings volatility of relying almost entirely on unsecured group lending.For bigger players, even a modest slice of a large balance sheet can be meaningful. CreditAccess Grameen's historical ROA has swung between 4-5 percent in good years and 1-2 percent in bad ones; the ambition behind its diversification push is a more consistent cross-cycle 4 percent.Another lesson that may matter as much as diversification is that the industry needs to know exactly who it's lending to. The multiple-lending problem was partly a failure of borrower identification."The need for a unique identifier is very important," says Baskar Babu R, MD of Suryoday Small Finance Bank. The industry is moving towards PAN and CKYC as the only acceptable borrower identifiers.The Road AheadFunding may determine which lenders emerge strongest. Demand returned strongly, capital was plentiful, new players entered and competition for borrowers intensified.
“Microfinance institutions were mono-line businesses for a long time due to regulatory prescription," says Ganesh Narayanan, CEO and MD of CreditAccess Grameen.
The problem was not just an external shock hitting an otherwise sound business; it was perhaps the first time, the sector itself had begun to overheat.
Lenders competed for customers already borrowing from several institutions, and indebtedness accumulated beneath what still looked like healthy growth.
At the peak, around a quarter of CreditAccess Grameen's AUM was linked to borrowers with exposure to more than three lenders; that figure is now around 2 percent.
The warning signs were visible in credit-bureau data, but the industry was slow to act.
When collections deteriorated in 2024, the first explanations were external—heat waves, elections, campaigns against indebtedness.
Then came the Karza Mukti Abhiyan and legislative intervention, most notably in Karnataka.
What looked like temporary disturbances exposed a deeper vulnerability: Credit had grown faster than the industry's ability to assess a household's total repayment capacity.
However, not all credit stress is the same.
A borrower hit by a drought can recover once the shock passes; a household that has taken on debt beyond what it can service faces a different problem entirely.
The industry spent much of the downturn figuring out which it was dealing with.
By the time leverage emerged as the bigger issue, lenders were already facing higher credit costs, weaker collections, tighter funding and a sceptical investor base.
In response, underwriting tightened, scrutiny of household indebtedness increased, and borrower-level monitoring strengthened.

But with cleaner credit metrics, can these businesses generate attractive returns without eventually recreating the same problem?

Borrowers Still Exist.
India's low-income households still need working capital, emergency finance, and money for housing and small businesses.
Moneylenders still operate alongside formal institutions, proof that demand in this segment far exceeds what the formal MFI industry serves.
Venkatesh Krishnan, CEO of Spandana Sphoorty, believes this is why microfinance will remain relevant for decades.
What has changed is the borrower.
A customer who enters the system with a Rs 30,000 joint-liability loan won't stay a microfinance customer forever.

stories.summary: Jerusalem, Oct 08: Israel said on Thursday that the British Consulate in east Jerusalem has “ceased to function” in that capacity and that 20 staffers would leave the country, the latest in what has been the biggest diplomatic friction between the close allies in decades. Britain said the building would continue to deliver “vital services” and work with Palestinians, and that it would not retaliate by expelling Israeli diplomats as it seeks to rebuild its staff. The sign outside the consulate was taken down. The dispute began last month when the United Kingdom banned trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank. The United Nations and much of the international community consider all settlements as illegal. “Israel will no longer turn its cheek to diplomatic attacks against it," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said in a statement, adding that the building would continue to operate with a “task force” of seven diplomats and a “very limited” scope of activity. Twenty British diplomats will leave Israel, including the consul general. British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said in a statement that the building "will be known as the UK Mission, Jerusalem” after discussions with Israel's government, and a small team of diplomats would continue to operate there. “This will ensure that we maintain our longstanding British presence and the UK's role in support of a two-state solution,” Miliband added. Britain had threatened to expel Israeli diplomats if the consulate was closed, but said it would not do so for now because it's in talks with Israel about increasing the UK presence at the mission. “We will work in the coming months to build back up our presence,” Miliband said. Meanwhile, “our diplomats are going to be able to carry out their important work in relation to, for example, relations with the Palestinians, but also supporting British nationals visiting the area,” Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty told Times Radio. Miliband made clear that Britain does “not accept that the government of Israel has the legal right to close the British Consulate General in Jerusalem, which has been there for nearly 200 years.” The foreign secretary added that the UK government reiterates its view that east Jerusalem "is occupied territory." Israel captured the West Bank, along with Gaza and East Jerusalem, in the 1967 Middle East war, territories the Palestinians want for a future state. Since then, the Israeli government has built scores of settlements that are home to well over 500,000 Jewish settlers. Many settlements resemble fully developed suburbs. The current government under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, the most nationalist and religious in Israel's history, views the West Bank as the biblical and historical homeland of the Jewish people and sees the settlements as key to maintaining security.

stories.headline: When Nana Patekar sought to join Army at Kargil front, spent 60 days with troops
stories.title: When Nana Patekar sought to join Army at Kargil front, spent 60 days with troops
stories.summary: Mumbai, Oct 8 : At the height of the Kargil War in 1999, Nana Patekar put his acting career on hold and sought permission to join the Indian Army at the war front, a chapter of his life that the veteran actor recalled years later during his appearance on "Kaun Banega Crorepati". Patekar, who died on Thursday at the age of 76 due to cardiac arrest in Goa, had rigourously trained with armed forces for his 1991 movie Prahaar: The Final Attack , in which he essayed the role of Major VS Chavan. He trained with the Maratha Light Infantry for three years for the film, which he had also written and directed. When the Kargil conflict broke out, Patekar approached senior army officers with a request to join the troops but was told that such permission could only be granted by the Defence Minister. "I knew our Defence Minister George Fernandes ji, so I called him. Even he said it was impossible," Patekar told megastar Amitabh Bachchan when he appeared on KBC in August 2024 when he was promoting the movie Vanvaas . "I told him, 'Commission toh six months mein hota hai, maine toh teen saal guzaare hain .' He asked where, and I told him about my experience with the Maratha Light Infantry. Then he asked, ' Kab jaana chahte ho? ' I told him, 'Today.'" The actor eventually received permission and travelled to the Kargil conflict zone in August 1999, where he spent time with Army personnel near the Line of Control. Patekar said he spent around 60 days with the troops during the conflict, travelling to places including Dras, Leh, Kupwara, Baramulla and Sopore. "I was 76 kg when I reached Srinagar. By the time I came back, I was 56 kg," he recalled. He said he was eventually a part of a Quick Reaction Team (QRT) and later helped at a military hospital in Srinagar. "There, the bodies of martyred soldiers were brought in. It was deeply distressing, as many of the bodies were in a bad state. The mortal remains were carefully made presentable before being sent back to their hometowns. I worked there for six days. "One day, I was roaming in the ward and one person shouted from behind, 'Hey Nana.' I knew that person and he was draped in a long sheet. I touched him and he was burning. He told me he had fever for past 4 days. He wanted go to back to battlefield but couldn't. He then showed that his legs were cut off," he recounted. For Patekar, it as an act of heroism but service to country. "I tell this to all actors. You have your own share of joys and sorrows in life. Keep performing from that space. Unless your definition of happiness and sorrow keeps changing, you won't be able to sustain yourself for long. "Go out and look around; there are all kinds of sorrows and joys. But your perception of happiness and sorrow should change," he said.

article_sentences: A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI), Surya Kant, and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana passed the directions while hearing a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) filed by disability rights lawyer Rahul Bajaj and child rights activist Zaheer Abbas Jan.

New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the Centre to collect and place on record state-wise information on the regulation, registration and monitoring of rehabilitation centres and other establishments catering to children with disabilities.

The CJI Kant-led Bench asked the Union government to coordinate with all states and Union Territories (UTs) and compile comprehensive data on the implementation of statutory safeguards governing such institutions.

The Supreme Court directed the Centre to place on record, by way of an affidavit, details regarding the constitution and functioning of statutory authorities under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (RPwD) Act, 2016, formulation and notification of minimum standards for mental health establishments, and the inspection and monitoring mechanisms in place for rehabilitation facilities.
During the hearing, Bajaj submitted that rehabilitation centres for Persons with Disabilities are required to obtain compulsory state-level registration under the RPwD Act.

He stressed the need for empirical data to ascertain whether the designated statutory authorities have actually been constituted across the states and whether they are actively discharging their regulatory and monitoring functions.
Averring to the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, Bajaj submitted that only 10 states and UTs have so far notified the requisite minimum standards for mental health establishments.

Taking note of the submissions, the CJI Kant-led Bench directed the Centre to coordinate with the state governments and UT administrations and furnish the requisite information before the Supreme Court.
The matter has been listed for further hearing on October 22.

The petition has highlighted alleged systemic failures in the implementation of statutory safeguards under the RPwD Act, the Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI) Act, 1992, and the Mental Healthcare Act.

According to the plea, despite the existing legislative framework, children with disabilities continue to face concerns arising from the functioning of unregistered institutions, inadequate infrastructure, shortage of qualified professionals and lack of effective regulatory oversight.

The petitioners had contended that institutions providing facilities to Persons with Disabilities are required to be registered under Section 50 of the RPwD Act, which prohibits any person from establishing or maintaining such an institution without obtaining a certificate of registration from the competent authority.

article_sentences: - TRAI Chairman Anil Kumar Lahoti said telecom tariffs are to be decided by operators under the current forbearance regime.
- TRAI will intervene on tariff hikes only when there is a necessity for regulatory action, Lahoti said.

The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) cannot act on “guesswork” over reports of a possible 10-15 percent telecom tariff hike, TRAI Chairman Anil Kumar Lahoti reportedly said, while reiterating that operators must comply with the regulator’s mandate to offer voice- and SMS-only plans despite industry pushback.
Speaking to CNBC-TV18, Lahoti said telecom tariffs are currently under a forbearance regime, under which operators are free to determine their prices.
He said market forces are driving tariffs in India’s competitive telecom sector, while TRAI continues to monitor developments.
“As far as tariff is concerned, as per the present regulatory provisions, the tariff is under forbearance, which means the tariff is to be decided by operators,” Lahoti reportedly said.
Asked whether TRAI would intervene if operators raised tariffs by 10-15 percent, Lahoti reportedly said, “I don’t think we can act on this based on guesswork.
As soon as there is a necessity of intervention, we’ll do that.”
He also pointed to the level of competition in the sector, saying tariffs in India are “probably the lowest in the world”.
On TRAI’s mandate for voice- and SMS-only plans, Lahoti reportedly said the regulator has not received a response from operators but stressed that the requirement is already part of the regulations.

“We haven’t received a response, but this is a regulation which has already been issued, and the operators are required to comply with this,” he was quoted as saying in a report dated October 6, 2026.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday (October 8, 2026) passed an interim order that the Udayasthamana Pooja must be held in accordance with the age-old practices of the famed Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple in Keralam.
A Bench headed by Justice Aravind Kumar remarked the faith and sentiments of worshippers must be given precedence over management hurdles.

The petitioners led by P.C. Hary and members of traditional managing families, represented by senior advocate Guru Krishnakumar, had challenged decisions by the Guruvayur devaswom managing committee to alter or reschedule the Udayasthamana Pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi.

The management, represented by senior advocates CA Sundaram, V. Giri and advocate Rohini Musa, had argued that the performance of the rituals during Ekadasi was faced by logistical challenges posed by the massive influx of devotees on that particular day.
“I have myself stood for seven hours,” Justice Kumar said, indicating it was part of the devotional expression.
The court said it would list the main appeal in December for final hearing.

The petitioners had moved the apex court after the Kerala High Court had dismissed their pleas for a direction to the temple devaswom to ensure the conduct of the Udayasthamana pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi.
In October last year, the apex court had passed a similar order allowing the conduct of the pooja on the Ekadasi day which fell in the month of November.
Mr. Hary had argued that the pooja was a sacred and integral part of the temple’s ritualistic tradition.

“Until 2023, the Udayasthamana pooja was invariably performed on Vrishchikam Ekadasi day, and it is only during the last two years, 2024 and 2025, that the respondents have attempted to alter this well-established religious practice.
Such arbitrary decisions by the respondents strike at the very root of the traditional practices of the temple, which have been observed for several centuries.
The Udayasthamana pooja on Vrishchikam Ekadasi is not merely symbolic but a series of nearly 15-18 poojas that are conducted from sunrise to sunset,” the petitioners had submitted.

article_sentences: The Supreme Court today called for suggestions on the creation of a dedicated corpus for providing financial assistance to people suffering from Spinal Muscular Atrophy, a rare genetic disorder.
A bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalya Bagchi and Justice V Mohana was dealing with a suo motu case taken up over lack of adequate and systematic treatment for SMA patients.
Senior Advocate Aparajita Singh (appointed as Amicus Curiae) and ASG Anil Kaushik appeared.

The case is an offshoot of the proceedings related to comedian Samay Raina and others, who were accused by M/s Cure SMA Foundation of making insensitive jokes about Persons with Disabilities (including those suffering from SMA).
After certain directions by the Court, the comedians apologized and took steps for making amends.
Thereafter, the proceedings were closed and the Court took up the present suo motu case to address the issue of systematic issues in treatment of SMA.
During today's hearing, the CJI asked the Union and the Amicus to suggest a proposal for establishing a dedicated corpus.
The judge expressed that the proposed corpus can include CSR contributions and government grants, but it should be permanent and not incidental in nature.
"it should not depend on the incidental circumstance that today CSR has come or upon persuasion, the government has released the grant...that should not be the case.
But what is the regular channel...a permanent system...kind of an automated nudge to contribution", CJI said.
The judge underlined that the focus should be more towards optimal utilization of the fund, instead of generating the fund.

stories.title: Supreme Court asks Centre to form panel to prevent pharma companies from indulging in unethical practices
stories.summary: The order was passed while hearing a 2021 petition filed by the Federation of Medical and Sales Representatives Association, which sought regulation of unethical marketing practices by pharmaceutical companies.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: The Supreme Court on Thursday directed the Centre to constitute a committee to consider suggestions on regulating pharmaceutical marketing practices and recommend measures to prevent drug companies from engaging in unethical practices.
A bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta said the committee would consider suggestions and representations before making recommendations to the government.
The Centre has also been directed to place the committee’s report before the court.
The matter has been listed for January 29 for consideration of the compliance affidavit to be filed by the Centre.

The order was passed while hearing a 2021 petition filed by the Federation of Medical and Sales Representatives Association, which sought regulation of unethical marketing practices by pharmaceutical companies.
The petition also raised alleged practices such as offering expensive gifts and other incentives to doctors to promote medicines.
The plea had sought directions from the Supreme Court to frame guidelines to control and regulate such practices until an effective law was enacted.

The Centre had told the court on September 8 that it was setting up a three-member panel to examine the issue and suggest a statutory framework to ensure pharmaceutical companies do not engage in unethical practices.
At the September hearing, the government had sought two months for the committee to submit its report, which would subsequently be placed before the Supreme Court for approval.
The Centre had acknowledged the need to strengthen the existing mechanism governing pharmaceutical marketing practices.
The government had said detailed discussions had taken place and the committee would examine whether a statutory framework was required and, if so, what form it should take.
Until the committee submits its report and a decision is taken on the proposed statutory framework, the Uniform Code for Pharmaceutical Marketing Practices, 2024, will continue to govern the sector.

stories.headline: INDIA bloc’s 12-hour bandh disrupts normal life across Odisha
stories.title: INDIA bloc’s 12-hour bandh disrupts normal life across Odisha
stories.summary: Bhubaneswar, Oct 8 : Normal life across Odisha was affected on Thursday due to the 12-hour statewide shutdown called by several opposition parties of the Congress-led INDIA bloc over four demands, including the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process. The 12-hour shutdown disrupted transportation services across the state as members of the communist parties, Congress and other political parties blocked National and State Highways by burning tyres on the roads at various places. Workers and leaders of the INDIA bloc staged picketing at important places in cities across the state. Youth Congress members also held bike rallies during the bandh. Passenger buses, auto-rickshaws and trucks were largely off the roads due to the bandh. Train services were also affected at several places for a few hours, while scuffles between security personnel and the INDIA bloc workers and leaders were reported from some locations as the latter tried to halt train services at railway stations. Hundreds of vehicles remained stranded on highways, causing massive inconvenience to commuters. Private institutions, business establishments and other establishments in major cities across Odisha also remained closed due to the bandh. Speaking to media persons, Odisha Pradesh Congress Committee (OPCC) president Bhakta Charan Das on Thursday said the 12-hour Odisha bandh called by the INDIA bloc was being observed peacefully across the state, with people extending support to the shutdown. Das said the bandh was being observed over four key demands, which include the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, repeal of the MMDR Amendment Act, 2026, resignation of Odisha School and Mass Education Minister Nityananda Gond over alleged errors in textbooks, and immediate relief and compensation for people affected by the recent floods in the state. “The impact of the bandh is more visible in rural areas than in cities. Schools, colleges, institutions, markets and transportation services have been affected across the state,” Das said. He said some relaxation had been given in Bhubaneswar to avoid inconvenience to tourists and people travelling from outside the state. Emergency services were also being allowed to operate. “We are observing the bandh peacefully and following the path of Mahatma Gandhi. There will be no violence,” he said, adding that he had repeatedly appealed to party workers and supporters to maintain peace. Das warned that if the government failed to address the four demands, the agitation would be intensified and could expand significantly over the next two months. --IANS

stories.headline: IMD Update: Widespread rain for TN, Kerala, Lakshadweep into weekend
stories.title: IMD Update: Widespread rain for TN, Kerala, Lakshadweep into weekend
stories.summary: South Peninsula turns stormy and rainy as easterly flow gathers pace across Bay of Bengal, signalling seasonal transition from south-west monsoon to north-east monsoon
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: After a lull of nearly a week, the south-west monsoon resumed its retreat on Thursday, withdrawing from the remaining parts of Maharashtra, as well as parts of Goa, Karnataka, Telangana and Odisha, and further areas of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh.

India Meteorological Department (IMD) said the withdrawal line now runs through Supaul, Ranchi, Sundargarh, Bargarh, Bijapur, Hyderabad, Belagavi and Panjim, marking another decisive step in the four-month monsoon’s seasonal retreat and arrival in turn of the monsoon in reverse, or north-east monsoon, over the South Peninsula.

Conditions are now becoming favourable for the monsoon to pull back from more parts of East India and the northern Peninsula, as well as many parts of the North-East, during the next three to four days.
But the retreating monsoon is leaving behind an atmosphere far from quiet, particularly over the southern Peninsula.
While the monsoon footprint contracts across the country, the seasonal transition is simultaneously opening the door to a more convective pattern over the South Peninsula.

Rain, thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds became entrenched on Thursday under the influence of a cyclonic circulation off the south Kerala coast and a trough extending into South Interior Karnataka.

Thus, even as the monsoon steadily retreats, the atmosphere remains primed for widespread pockets of rain and thunderstorms, a characteristic feature of the transitional season when the monsoon’s withdrawal from the north coincides with renewed convective activity over the South Peninsula and adjoining regions.
The pattern is expected to persist for much of the coming week.
Isolated to scattered rainfall is likely over Coastal Andhra Pradesh and Yanam, Coastal Karnataka, Rayalaseema, South Interior Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal for next seven days.
Kerala and Mahe may see a similar unsettled spell for three days from Sunday, while Lakshadweep could remain under its influence for four days.

Rainfall may be fairly widespread to widespread over Kerala and Mahe until Sunday, with another spell likely on Wednesday, while Lakshadweep could receive fairly widespread to widespread rain for three days through Sunday.
The heavier spells could be locally significant.
